opus-5.5.text:
I think Pi is one of the most important teams in the field right now, and the reason isn't any single demo. It's that they've been very clear about the bet they're making: that robotics can follow a path similar to language models, where you build one general foundation model trained on a huge diversity of data, and then adapt it to many embodiments and tasks, instead of building a separate system for every robot and every job.

When π0 came out, what impressed me wasn't just the laundry folding or the box assembly, though those are genuinely hard, long-horizon, deformable-object tasks that the field struggled with for years. It was the architecture choice. They took a pretrained vision-language model as the backbone and attached an action expert using flow matching, so you get the semantic understanding from internet-scale pretraining plus smooth, high-frequency continuous control. That's a very pragmatic combination. Then with π0.5 they pushed further on generalization, putting robots into homes they had never seen before, which is really the question everyone cares about. Can it work outside the lab?

Their team composition matters too. You have people like Sergey Levine and Chelsea Finn, who have spent more than a decade on robot learning, together with people who understand large-scale model training. In embodied AI you need both: deep intuition about what goes wrong on real hardware, and the engineering discipline to scale data and compute.

That said, I'd keep a few things in perspective. First, data is still the bottleneck. Language models had the whole internet; robotics doesn't have an equivalent. Pi collects a lot of teleoperation data across different robots, but it's expensive, and nobody has proven yet what the scaling curve really looks like for physical data. Second, demo success rates and deployment reliability are very different things. A 70 or 80 percent success rate is a great research result, but a customer in a factory or a home needs something much closer to 99.9 percent, and the last few nines are usually where the real difficulty is. Third, there's an open question about whether the "brain" can be fully separated from the "body." Pi is betting heavily on cross-embodiment generalization, which I think is directionally right, but hardware still constrains what's possible, especially in dexterity and tactile sensing.

So my overall view is that Pi is defining the research agenda for embodied foundation models, and they're making the field more open by releasing models and sharing results, which helps everyone. But we're still in the GPT-2 era of robotics, maybe GPT-2-and-a-half. The direction is becoming clearer, while the commercial path and the true scaling laws are still being written. For teams in China, this is actually an opportunity, because we have strong advantages in hardware supply chains and in real deployment scenarios, and those are exactly where the data will eventually come from.

fable-5.1.text:
Pi is probably the most important company in the space right now, and I say that even though I think several of their core bets are still open questions.

What they got right first is the framing. Before Pi, a lot of robot learning was still organized around tasks: here is a model for folding, here is a model for grasping. Pi came in with the position that the robot problem is a foundation model problem, that you train one policy on as much heterogeneous data as you can get across many embodiments, and that the generalization will come from scale and diversity rather than from clever task-specific engineering. The pi-zero work, and then the follow-ups, made that argument concrete. The laundry folding and box-assembly demos mattered less as capabilities than as evidence that a single generalist policy could do long-horizon, dexterous, contact-rich things that people used to assume needed hand-built pipelines.

The second thing they got right is the architecture choice of starting from a vision-language model and bolting on an action head, with flow matching for continuous control. That sounds like a small decision, but it let them inherit the semantic understanding of the pretrained VLM and spend their robot data on learning motion rather than learning what a towel is. The later work on open-world generalization, where the robot goes into homes it has never seen, is really the test of whether that inheritance holds up, and the results there were more convincing than I expected.

Where I am more cautious is on three points. First, data. Their edge is that they collected a very large, very diverse teleoperation dataset, and that is expensive and slow. The question is whether that is a scaling law like language, where more data keeps paying off, or whether it saturates and you need a different source like simulation or video. They clearly believe the former, and the jury is still out.

Second, embodiment. Cross-embodiment training is elegant, but every time you add a new robot you still need a meaningful amount of data on that specific body. The dream of "download the model, plug in your arm" is not here yet.

Third, the business. Pi has been disciplined about staying a model company and not a robot company, licensing to hardware partners. I think that is the right call intellectually, but it means their success depends on someone else building the hardware and the deployments. That is a bet that the ecosystem matures around them.

So my assessment is: they set the agenda, they have the strongest research team doing this work in public, and they moved the field from "can a learned policy do this at all" to "how well does it generalize." Whether they become the OpenAI of robotics or the group that proves the thesis and then gets outscaled by someone with more data and more hardware is, I think, genuinely undecided.

astra-6.text:
I think Pi is pursuing an important idea: can we build a model that learns broadly useful physical skills, rather than train a separate system for every task? That’s an ambitious direction, because a robot has to connect perception and reasoning with actions that work in the real world.

What interests me most is whether those capabilities transfer. If you change the object, the environment, or the task, can the system adapt without extensive retraining? And when something goes wrong, can it recognize the failure and recover? A successful demonstration is encouraging, but consistent performance under those changes is a much stronger test.

So I’m optimistic about the direction, but I’d distinguish the promise of embodied foundation models from proof that we have a general-purpose robot. My assessment would depend on how reliably Pi’s models generalize, how much new data they need, and how much human intervention remains necessary.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d assess Pi along two dimensions: whether its models can generalize, and whether that generalization makes robots useful in practice.

For an embodied foundation model, the key question is what happens outside the training setup. Can it handle a new object, a different room, or an instruction it hasn’t encountered before? And when something goes wrong, can it recover? A successful demonstration is encouraging, but repeated performance under changing conditions is much stronger evidence.

There’s also the question of how much adaptation each new task requires. If you still need extensive data collection and engineering for every deployment, the benefits of a foundation model are limited. If that effort falls substantially as the model improves, that’s a meaningful advance.

So I find the direction compelling. But I would judge Pi by reliability, transfer, and the cost of deployment. Those are the measures that will tell us how far embodied foundation models have actually progressed.
